project.name: whatthefuckshouldiwatch
project.description: moviePicker is a browser-based movie discovery app with a small Node HTTP server serving the frontend and `/api/*` endpoints. It supports anonymous browsing, Google sign-in and sessions, account-backed saved titles and people with localStorage fallback, TMDb/OMDb integrations with demo fallback, PostgreSQL-backed people ingestion, Render deployment, and GitHub Actions.

tour.title: Project and Runtime
tour.description: The README introduces moviePicker as a live movie-discovery application with optional account-backed data, an offline people pipeline, and a Render/Postgres deployment path. The server entry point turns that product map into a hardened Node HTTP service, combining static delivery, TMDb/OMDb discovery, authentication, saved-data APIs, database reads, caching, and local fallbacks. Together they provide the orientation needed for every later stop.

tour.title: Discovery Page
tour.description: With the server boundary established, the main HTML page and app.js form the browser entry point for discovery. The markup supplies navigation, filters, result rails, templates, and account controls, while the controller manages URL-backed search state, data bootstrapping, enrichment, rendering, and saves. The shared stylesheet makes that multi-part experience responsive and accessible across screen sizes.

tour.title: Shared Browser Services
tour.description: The discovery page relies on three high-fan-in browser modules that keep identity, persistence, and movie presentation consistent across pages. auth-client.js bootstraps Google-backed session state, saved-data-client.js chooses localStorage or CSRF-protected account storage, and movie-results.js centralizes safe card rendering and progressive enrichment. These modules are the connective tissue for the feature pages that follow.
tour.languageLesson: In a vanilla multi-page JavaScript application, shared scripts can expose a small browser API and publish state changes as events, allowing separate page controllers to stay decoupled while reusing session and persistence behavior.

tour.title: People and Studio Search
tour.description: Building on the shared renderers and saved-data client, the people page supports accessible directories plus person- and studio-centered movie searches. people.js coordinates URL-backed filters, navigation state, saved actions, movie rails, and title enrichment, while catalog-search.js provides reusable search-form initialization and redirects into the main results flow. This is the second major discovery path alongside the title-first experience from Step 2.

tour.title: Saved Libraries
tour.description: The saved-title and saved-people workspaces turn discovery results into durable personal collections. Their page shells define accessible rails and tabbed views, while their controllers render, enrich, remove, and reorganize items through the shared clients from Step 3. The same UI therefore works with anonymous browser storage or signed-in server synchronization.

tour.title: Account and Sessions
tour.description: The account page extends saved collections into a signed-in control surface for profile details, synced-library totals, and active browser sessions. account.js loads those views and performs CSRF-aware revocation of one session or all other sessions. This browser workflow is the visible end of the authentication services explored next.

tour.title: Identity and Sessions
tour.description: Following the server's direct dependencies, Google token verification and transactional user linking establish who a visitor is. The session service then creates hashed opaque tokens, resolves request identity, revokes sessions, and delegates cookie formatting to a focused utility. These modules form the first-party security boundary beneath the account experience from Step 6.
tour.languageLesson: Small CommonJS modules keep security responsibilities narrow: identity verification, persistence, token lifecycle, and cookie serialization can evolve and be tested without being embedded in the main HTTP router.

tour.title: Request and Data Guards
tour.description: The remaining server helpers protect state-changing requests and keep account data bounded. HTTP utilities limit JSON bodies and normalize proxy-aware request context, origin guards enforce the trusted-site allowlist, and CSRF tokens are bound to sessions and compared safely. Separate stores persist saved items and summarize account holdings without moving database logic into the central server file.

tour.title: Authentication Data Model
tour.description: The authentication roadmap explains how the browser and server pieces were staged toward Google sign-in, first-party sessions, and cross-device saved data. Its SQL schema supplies the persistent users, external identities, sessions, saved titles, and saved people used by the services in Steps 7 and 8. Cascade relationships and lookup indexes make lifecycle operations and account queries explicit at the database boundary.
tour.languageLesson: Relational schemas use foreign keys and cascades to enforce ownership and cleanup rules, while targeted indexes keep identity, session, and saved-library lookups efficient.

tour.title: Pipeline Data Foundation
tour.description: A separate Postgres schema models ingestion runs, queued people, normalized movies and credits, recognition ranks, and published snapshots for fast reads. Shared helpers supply TMDb access, export streaming, concurrency control, database pools, schema application, and ranking queries. This foundation separates repeatable ingestion mechanics from the long-running worker and one-shot jobs in the next step.
tour.languageLesson: An ingestion schema separates raw queue state from normalized entities and published read models, allowing workers to resume safely while the web application consumes stable snapshots.

tour.title: People Pipeline Lifecycle
tour.description: The worker turns the Step 10 foundation into a continuous data lifecycle: source IDs are queued, profiles and credits are hydrated, recognition signals are refreshed, and site snapshots are published. auto-pipeline.js schedules that cycle, while focused scripts keep each stage runnable and observable on its own. The result is a prepared people catalog that supports responsive discovery without rebuilding rankings during each browser request.

tour.title: Security Verification
tour.description: The hardening test suite closes the application loop by exercising the security boundaries introduced in Steps 7 through 9. It checks cookies, trusted origins, CSRF, saved-data normalization, database writes, static-file allowlisting, HTTP methods, query defaults, and response headers. Reading it after the implementation reveals the guarantees the system treats as non-negotiable.

tour.title: Configuration and Delivery
tour.description: The final stop shows how the application, worker, database, and external services are configured and shipped. package.json defines the Node runtime commands, .env.example documents required provider and security settings, and render.yaml provisions the web service, ingestion worker, and Postgres environment. The deployment helper and GitHub Actions workflow coordinate validated web-and-worker releases, completing the path from local entry point to production.
tour.languageLesson: Declarative YAML records service topology and environment wiring, while the deployment script handles procedural checks and hook calls; keeping those roles separate makes production intent reviewable.
